questions.stem: When the Republic of China was proclaimed on 1 January 1912, its provisional president in Nanjing was:
options: Jiang Jieshi (Chiang Kai-shek)
Chen Duxiu (Ch'en Tu-hsiu)
Sun Yixian (Sun Yat-sen)
Yuan Shikai (Yuan Shih-k'ai)
questions.explanation: Sun, the leader of the Revolutionary Alliance, returned from abroad and was chosen provisional president after the 1911 revolution. Within weeks he gave way to Yuan Shikai, the most powerful general in the north.

questions.stem: Sun Yixian handed the presidency to Yuan Shikai in 1912 mainly because Yuan:
options: had personally led the Wuchang Uprising that began the 1911 revolution
commanded the strongest army and could secure the emperor's abdication
had won the first national elections for the new Republic's parliament
had founded the Revolutionary Alliance and written its political programme
questions.explanation: Yuan controlled the Beiyang Army, and in return for the presidency he arranged the abdication of the child emperor Puyi in February 1912. The Guomindang, not Yuan, won the elections held over the winter of 1912–13.

questions.stem: The assassination of Song Jiaoren in March 1913 was significant because Song:
options: had led the Guomindang to victory in the parliamentary elections
had been chosen by Yuan Shikai to succeed him as emperor of China
had founded the Chinese Communist Party in Shanghai the year before
had been the commander of the Republic's army in the Northern Expedition
questions.explanation: Song organised the Guomindang into a parliamentary party that won the 1912–13 elections, and he expected to lead the government. His murder, widely blamed on Yuan, ended hopes of parliamentary rule and led to the failed 'Second Revolution'.

questions.stem: Which actions by Yuan Shikai most clearly undermined the early Republic?
options: Launching the Northern Expedition against the warlords who controlled the north
Forming the First United Front with the Communist Party and the Soviet Union
Banning the Guomindang, dissolving parliament and declaring himself emperor
Signing the Treaty of Versailles, which transferred Shandong's rights to Japan
questions.explanation: Yuan crushed the 1913 'Second Revolution', banned the Guomindang, dissolved parliament and in late 1915 proclaimed a new imperial dynasty, abandoning it in 1916 shortly before his death. He died in 1916, before Versailles, and China refused to sign that treaty.

questions.stem: Yuan Shikai's acceptance of most of Japan's Twenty-One Demands in 1915:
options: secured the return of Shandong from Germany to China
forced Japan to withdraw all of its forces from Manchuria
won the backing of Britain for a constitutional monarchy
damaged his standing and inflamed Chinese nationalism
questions.explanation: The Demands sought to make China a virtual Japanese protectorate, and Yuan's acceptance of a modified version was seen as a national humiliation. Japan was taking over Germany's Shandong rights, not returning them to China.

questions.stem: After Yuan Shikai's death in 1916, China entered a period in which:
options: the Chinese Communist Party controlled the countryside through peasant soviets
regional warlords fought for control and the Beijing government had little real power
the Guomindang ruled a united China from Nanjing under a new democratic constitution
Japan governed all of northern China directly through a puppet emperor in Beijing
questions.explanation: In the warlord era, generals with private armies controlled provinces, taxed and fought each other, while governments in Beijing changed often and depended on them. Unifying China against the warlords became the Guomindang's aim.

questions.stem: The New Culture Movement called for 'Mr Science and Mr Democracy' to replace:
options: Soviet-style Marxism-Leninism
the Guomindang's one-party state
the rule of the foreign treaty-port concessions
Confucian tradition and its values
questions.explanation: Writers in Chen Duxiu's magazine New Youth, founded in 1915, blamed Confucian hierarchy, filial obedience and old learning for China's weakness. Marxism-Leninism became popular among some of them only after 1919.

questions.stem: Lu Xun's story 'A Madman's Diary' (1918), written in vernacular Chinese, attacked:
options: the Japanese occupation of Manchuria and the puppet state there
the Guomindang's New Life Movement and its rules on behaviour
traditional Confucian society as one that devoured its own people
the Communist Party's land reforms in the Jiangxi Soviet's villages
questions.explanation: The narrator sees the words 'eat people' between the lines of the classics, a metaphor for a culture that crushed individuals. The story was a landmark of the New Culture Movement; the Jiangxi Soviet, Manchukuo and New Life all came in the 1930s.

questions.stem: The May Fourth demonstrations of 1919 began with student protests in Beijing against:
options: Japan's invasion and occupation of Manchuria following the Mukden Incident
the Versailles decision to give Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan
Yuan Shikai's plan to restore the monarchy with himself as emperor
the Guomindang's massacre of communists and workers in Shanghai
questions.explanation: Students learned that the Allies at Versailles would transfer Germany's concessions in Shandong to Japan, and protests spread to strikes and boycotts across China. The other events belong to 1915, 1927 and 1931.

questions.stem: Why do historians see the May Fourth Movement as a turning point for Chinese communism?
options: Sun Yixian joined the communists and made Marxism the Guomindang's official creed
It led directly to Japan's withdrawal from Shandong and its defeat in Manchuria
Anger at the Western powers turned many radicals towards Marxism and the Russian example
It forced the warlord government in Beijing to admit the communists to its cabinet
questions.explanation: The betrayal at Versailles discredited Western liberal models for many young intellectuals, while the Bolsheviks offered to renounce Tsarist privileges in China. Figures such as Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu and Mao turned to Marxism, and the CCP was founded in 1921.

questions.stem: Sun Yixian's Three Principles of the People are:
options: nationalism, democracy and the people's livelihood
science, democracy and the rejection of Confucianism
liberty, equality and fraternity for all citizens
unity, discipline and loyalty to the party leader
questions.explanation: The Three Principles (Sanmin zhuyi) were minzu (nationalism), minquan (democracy or people's rights) and minsheng (people's livelihood). 'Science and democracy' was the New Culture Movement's slogan, and liberty, equality and fraternity were French revolutionary ideals.

questions.stem: Sun Yixian's principle of the people's livelihood (minsheng) was concerned mainly with:
options: restoring Confucian rites, family loyalty and respect for one's elders
economic welfare, including equal land rights and regulating capital
ending foreign imperialism and earlier the rule of the Manchu Qing
elections, a constitution and five separate branches of government
questions.explanation: Minsheng aimed at a fair economy, for example equalising land rights so that rising land values benefited society and limiting private capital. Ending imperialism was the principle of nationalism, and a constitution with five branches was part of democracy.

questions.stem: Sun argued that China would reach constitutional government only after stages of military unification and 'political tutelage'. Jiang Jieshi later used this idea to justify:
options: handing power back to the northern warlords
one-party Guomindang rule during the Nanjing Decade
a coalition government with the Communist Party
immediate national elections held in 1928
questions.explanation: After unification in 1928, the Guomindang declared the period of political tutelage, under which the party ruled on the people's behalf until they were judged ready for democracy. In practice the promised constitutional stage was repeatedly delayed.

questions.stem: In his 1927 Report on the Peasant Movement in Hunan, Mao wrote that 'a revolution is not a dinner party' and defended peasant attacks on landlords. This source best shows Mao's:
options: acceptance of violent class struggle led by the poor peasants
commitment to peaceful change through parliamentary elections
loyalty to Jiang Jieshi's leadership of the national revolution
belief that the urban workers alone could lead the revolution
questions.explanation: Mao argued the peasants would rise 'like a mighty storm' and that the violence of peasant associations was necessary to overthrow landlord power. Seeing the peasants rather than urban workers as the main force was the core of his break with orthodox thinking.

questions.stem: Mao Zedong Thought differed most from Soviet-style Marxism-Leninism in its:
options: reliance on the peasants and rural bases rather than urban workers
rejection of a disciplined party to lead the revolutionary masses
belief that capitalism must fully develop before any revolution
rejection of armed struggle in favour of winning elections
questions.explanation: Mao adapted Marxism to China by making the peasantry the main revolutionary force and surrounding the cities from the countryside. He kept Lenin's disciplined party and armed struggle, and did not wait for capitalism to mature.

questions.stem: Mao's guerrilla principle 'The enemy advances, we retreat; the enemy camps, we harass; the enemy tires, we attack; the enemy retreats, we pursue' was designed to:
options: hold fixed defensive lines around the cities
avoid any contact with the enemy's forces
let a weaker army wear down a stronger one
win the war in one decisive pitched battle
questions.explanation: The principle, developed in the Jinggang Mountains and Jiangxi, used mobility, local knowledge and peasant support to strike where the enemy was weak. Fixed defensive lines were what the Red Army tried in 1934, with disastrous results.

questions.stem: The 'mass line' in Mao Zedong Thought meant that party cadres should:
options: restrict political work to educated urban workers and students
gather the ideas of the masses, refine them, and return them as policy
follow the Comintern's instructions without consulting the peasants
leave policy entirely to elected peasant assemblies in each village
questions.explanation: The mass line, summed up as 'from the masses, to the masses', meant cadres living among the people, learning their concerns and turning them into party policy that they then explained back. It kept leadership firmly in party hands while building popular support.

questions.stem: In On New Democracy (1940), Mao proposed that after victory China would be governed by:
options: a dictatorship of the industrial proletariat that would abolish private business at once
a parliamentary democracy in which the CCP and Guomindang shared power equally
a restored constitutional monarchy under the last Qing emperor, Puyi
a coalition of revolutionary classes, including the national bourgeoisie, led by the CCP
questions.explanation: New Democracy promised an alliance of workers, peasants, petty bourgeoisie and national bourgeoisie under communist leadership, with private business tolerated for a time. This reassured moderates, and it shaped the Common Programme of 1949.

questions.stem: Under the First United Front, members of the Chinese Communist Party:
options: joined the Guomindang as individuals while keeping their own party
dissolved their party and merged it completely into the Guomindang
formed a separate northern government in alliance with the warlords
took over the Guomindang's leadership after Sun Yixian's death
questions.explanation: On Comintern advice, communists entered the Guomindang as individual members from 1923–24 while the CCP continued as a separate party. This 'bloc within' strategy grew the CCP but left it exposed when Jiang turned on it.

questions.stem: The Northern Expedition launched from Guangzhou in 1926 aimed to:
options: drive the Japanese army out of Manchuria and Shandong
destroy the communist base areas in Jiangxi province
escort the Red Army safely north to Shaanxi province
defeat the warlords and unify China under the Guomindang
questions.explanation: The National Revolutionary Army under Jiang, with communist organisers stirring up workers and peasants ahead of it, took Wuhan, Shanghai and Nanjing by 1927 and Beijing in 1928. The Jiangxi base areas and the Long March came later.

questions.stem: In April 1927 Jiang Jieshi turned on the communists and the workers' unions in Shanghai with the help of:
options: the Red Army forces commanded by Zhu De
the Soviet adviser Mikhail Borodin
the Japanese navy's ships moored in the Huangpu River
the Green Gang and other underworld groups
questions.explanation: Jiang used Green Gang gunmen, backed by Shanghai's bankers and businessmen, to attack the communist-led unions; many were killed in the White Terror that followed. Borodin was the Comintern's adviser to the Guomindang and was forced to leave China later that year.

questions.stem: Which factor best explains why Jiang Jieshi broke with the communists in 1927?
options: Stalin had instructed the communists to leave the United Front at once
He feared communist-led workers and peasants threatened his allies and power
Sun Yixian had ordered the communists expelled shortly before his death
The communists had refused to take part in the Northern Expedition
questions.explanation: Strikes and peasant uprisings organised by communists alarmed the landlords, merchants and officers who supported Jiang, and he saw the CCP as a rival for control of the Guomindang. Sun had backed the United Front, and Stalin wanted the CCP to stay in it.

questions.stem: After the failure of the Autumn Harvest Uprising in 1927, Mao led his remaining forces to:
options: Moscow to train at the Comintern's school for cadres
the Jinggang Mountains on the Hunan–Jiangxi border
the city of Yan'an in the north of Shaanxi province
the Shanghai factories to organise the city's workers
questions.explanation: In the Jinggang Mountains Mao joined with Zhu De to build a rural base and the Red Army, the start of his strategy of revolution from the countryside. Yan'an became the base only after the Long March.

questions.stem: The Chinese Soviet Republic, proclaimed in November 1931 with Mao as chairman, had its capital at:
options: Yan'an in Shaanxi
Nanjing in Jiangsu
Wuhan in Hubei
Ruijin in Jiangxi
questions.explanation: The Jiangxi Soviet at Ruijin carried out land redistribution and built the Red Army, surviving several Guomindang encirclement campaigns. Nanjing was the Guomindang's capital, and Yan'an the CCP base after 1935.

questions.stem: Which was an achievement of the Guomindang government during the Nanjing Decade?
options: Defeating Japan and recovering Manchuria for the Republic
Building roads and railways and regaining control of China's tariffs
Carrying out land reform that gave farmland to the tenant farmers
Ending corruption among officials and in the National Army
questions.explanation: The Nanjing government extended roads and railways, won tariff autonomy from the foreign powers and reformed the currency in 1935. It largely avoided land reform, corruption remained widespread, and Manchuria stayed under Japanese control.

questions.stem: Lloyd Eastman, a historian critical of the Nanjing Decade, argued that the Guomindang failed mainly because:
options: it handed power to the communists after the Xi'an Incident of 1936
it relied on elections in the provinces that the warlords controlled
it neglected rural reform and was weakened by corruption and factionalism
it carried out land reform too quickly for the landlords who backed it
questions.explanation: In The Abortive Revolution and Seeds of Destruction, Eastman argued that the Guomindang decayed from within, failing to address peasant poverty and becoming corrupt and factional. Land reform was precisely what it avoided.

questions.stem: The New Life Movement, launched in 1934 by Jiang Jieshi and Song Meiling, promoted:
options: Confucian virtues, discipline and personal hygiene
Marxist class struggle against village landlords
vernacular literature and freedom in marriage
democratic elections to the provincial assemblies
questions.explanation: New Life drew on the Confucian virtues of propriety, righteousness, integrity and a sense of shame, with rules on cleanliness, dress and behaviour such as not spitting. It aimed at moral renewal and national discipline, not social or political reform.

questions.stem: The New Life Movement is often judged to have had little effect because it:
options: redistributed too much land too quickly to the poorest peasant families
was run by the Communist Party and so was rejected by the Guomindang
was banned by Japan in the parts of China under Japanese occupation
set rules for personal behaviour while ignoring poverty and land hunger
questions.explanation: Asking peasants to button their collars and stop spitting did nothing about rents, debt or hunger, so the movement seemed irrelevant to most Chinese. It was a Guomindang campaign and involved no land redistribution.

questions.stem: The CCP abandoned the Jiangxi Soviet in October 1934 mainly because:
options: Stalin ordered the Red Army to withdraw to the Soviet border in Xinjiang
the Guomindang had agreed to a Second United Front and wanted the area
Jiang's fifth encirclement campaign used blockhouses to tighten a blockade
Japanese forces advanced south from Manchuria and invaded Jiangxi province
questions.explanation: The fifth campaign surrounded the Soviet with fortified blockhouses and cut off supplies, while the party leaders and the Comintern adviser Otto Braun abandoned guerrilla tactics for costly positional warfare. The Japanese did not reach Jiangxi until the late 1930s.

questions.stem: The Zunyi Conference of January 1935 was significant because:
options: Mao gained a leading role in military affairs as the Comintern-backed leaders lost ground
Mao was elected chairman of the Chinese People's Republic and its army
the CCP agreed to form the Second United Front against Japan with Jiang Jieshi
the Red Army decided to return to Jiangxi and break the Guomindang blockade
questions.explanation: At Zunyi the leadership of Bo Gu and Otto Braun was blamed for the losses in Jiangxi, and Mao joined the top leadership with a major say in military strategy. His formal supremacy came later, and the People's Republic was not proclaimed until 1949.

questions.stem: Although the Red Army lost most of its soldiers on the Long March, historians see it as significant mainly because it:
options: secured Mao's leadership and became a lasting legend of CCP endurance
defeated the Guomindang's main armies in a series of decisive battles
won the support of the Soviet Union, which sent troops to defend Yan'an
ended the Japanese occupation of northern China within two years
questions.explanation: The March preserved the party's core leadership and was turned into a heroic story; Mao called it a manifesto, a propaganda force and a seeding machine. It was a retreat, not a series of victories, and the Soviets sent no troops.

questions.stem: Jung Chang and Jon Halliday's Mao: The Unknown Story challenged the CCP's heroic account of the Long March by arguing that:
options: the Long March was a Guomindang operation later renamed by Mao
the famous battle for the Luding Bridge was largely invented
the Red Army had in fact marched south to the island of Hainan
Mao was absent from the march and remained hidden in Shanghai
questions.explanation: Chang and Halliday, who are highly critical of Mao, claimed there was no real battle at the Luding Bridge over the Dadu River and that Jiang allowed the Reds to escape. Their claims are disputed by other historians, but the argument is theirs.

questions.stem: After the Mukden Incident of September 1931, Japan:
options: occupied Manchuria and set up the puppet state of Manchukuo
withdrew its forces from China under pressure from the League
signed an alliance with the Guomindang against the communists
invaded Jiangxi to destroy the Chinese Soviet Republic at Ruijin
questions.explanation: Japanese officers staged an explosion on the railway near Mukden as a pretext, and Japan's army took over Manchuria, installing the last Qing emperor Puyi as head of Manchukuo in 1932. The League condemned this in the Lytton Report and Japan left the League.

questions.stem: Jiang Jieshi's policy after 1931 of 'first internal pacification, then external resistance' meant:
options: handing Manchuria to Japan in exchange for Soviet aid
leaving defence to the warlords while reforming the army
destroying the communists before fully resisting Japan
making peace with the communists to fight Japan at once
questions.explanation: Jiang believed China had to be unified before it could fight Japan, so his best troops attacked the Red Army. Many Chinese saw this as appeasement, which helped the CCP present itself as the true patriotic force.

questions.stem: In the Xi'an Incident of December 1936, Jiang Jieshi was:
options: detained by his own generals until he agreed to unite with the CCP against Japan
captured by Mao's Red Army on its way north at the end of the Long March
wounded by Japanese bombers while visiting his troops in northern Shaanxi
removed as leader of the Guomindang by a vote of its Central Executive Committee
questions.explanation: Zhang Xueliang, the 'Young Marshal' driven out of Manchuria by Japan, and Yang Hucheng held Jiang until he agreed to end the civil war; Zhou Enlai took part in the talks. The Long March had ended in 1935.

questions.stem: Why was the Xi'an Incident so important for the CCP?
options: It caused Japan to recognise the CCP as the legal government of the north
It ended the Guomindang's campaign to destroy it and gave it time to grow
It made Mao the head of a joint government with the Guomindang in Nanjing
It brought Soviet troops into China to defend the communist base areas
questions.explanation: The Second United Front, formalised after the Japanese invasion of 1937, ended the encirclement campaigns, gave the CCP legal standing and let it expand behind Japanese lines. The CCP never joined a government in Nanjing.

questions.stem: During the war with Japan, the CCP's Rectification Movement of 1942–44 in Yan'an:
options: introduced free elections between the CCP and Guomindang in the base areas
returned land confiscated from landlords in Jiangxi to its original owners
brought Soviet advisers to Yan'an to run the party's military operations
enforced loyalty to Mao's thought through study, self-criticism and purges
questions.explanation: Party members studied Mao's writings, confessed errors and were investigated, and critics such as the writer Wang Shiwei were punished. It made Mao's ideas party orthodoxy, written into the CCP constitution in 1945.

questions.stem: Mao's Talks at the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art (1942) declared that art and literature should:
options: be written for an educated urban readership in foreign styles
serve the workers, peasants and soldiers and the revolution
be free from political control so that artists could criticise
copy the classical Confucian forms of the imperial examinations
questions.explanation: Mao said there was no art for art's sake: writers must serve the masses and the party's political aims. The Talks ended the freedom some Yan'an writers had used to criticise the party, and became the basis of cultural policy after 1949.

questions.stem: During the war against Japan, the CCP in its base areas mostly limited land policy to reducing rents and interest rather than confiscating land. The main reason was to:
options: comply with Japanese occupation laws that forbade redistributing land
keep landlords and richer peasants within the anti-Japanese united front
obey a Comintern ban on all land reform in China for the length of the war
satisfy poor peasants, who were firmly opposed to any cut in their rents
questions.explanation: Moderate reform improved poor peasants' lives without driving landlords and rich peasants into the enemy camp. Once the Civil War began, the CCP returned to radical land confiscation in the areas it controlled.

questions.stem: Chalmers Johnson argued that the CCP won mass support mainly by leading peasant resistance to Japan. Which historian challenged this with the view that support came chiefly from the party's social and economic reforms in its base areas?
options: Richard Pipes
Mark Selden
Lloyd Eastman
Jung Chang
questions.explanation: In The Yenan Way in Revolutionary China, Selden emphasised rent reduction, cooperatives and mass mobilisation in Yan'an as the key to CCP support. Eastman studied the Guomindang's failings, and Pipes wrote on Russia.

questions.stem: Which wartime development did most to weaken the Guomindang before the Civil War?
options: Winning the war against Japan on its own and then sharing power with the communists
Receiving no foreign aid at all during the war and having to disband its army
Carrying out radical land reform that turned the landlords against the government
Losing its eastern cities, suffering soaring inflation and the defeats of the 1944 Ichigo Offensive
questions.explanation: Driven back to Chongqing, the Guomindang lost its main tax base and printed money, causing inflation, while corruption and conscription abuses spread and the Ichigo Offensive inflicted heavy losses. The United States gave substantial aid, and it avoided land reform.

questions.stem: Which factor helped the CCP win the Civil War of 1946–49?
options: The Soviet army occupied Nanjing and installed Mao as leader
Land reform in the areas it held won peasant recruits and supplies
American troops fought alongside the People's Liberation Army
The Guomindang's armies were smaller and less well equipped from the start
questions.explanation: Redistributing land gave peasants a stake in communist victory, providing soldiers, porters and grain. The Guomindang began the war with larger and better-equipped forces, and the United States supported Jiang, not the CCP.

questions.stem: On 1 October 1949 in Beijing, Mao Zedong proclaimed:
options: the start of the Second United Front with Jiang
the creation of the Chinese Soviet Republic
the launch of the first encirclement campaign
the founding of the People's Republic of China
questions.explanation: Mao proclaimed the People's Republic from the Gate of Heavenly Peace (Tiananmen), and Jiang's government retreated to Taiwan by the end of 1949. The Chinese Soviet Republic was proclaimed at Ruijin in 1931.
